newsitem.title: USA: Why NATO at issue as Clinton sells expansion.
newsitem.headline: Why NATO at issue as Clinton sells expansion.

text.p: After NATO's decision to bring in three former communist states, U.S. President Bill Clinton must win backing for the idea from the American people, including some who question why the alliance is needed at all in post-Cold War era.
U.S. officials and scholars have argued over the fine points of NATO enlargement with increasing intensity for more than three years and there is still much division among them.

Until now, the American public has been largely unaffected and unconcerned by the debate, which has taken place at think tanks, in government offices, on the editorial pages of major newspapers and in foreign policy journals.

But with NATO's formal decision this week to invite Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic to join the alliance, the issue goes to the U.S. Senate for approval -- and hence Clinton and his aides must reach out to the voters who elect the senators and influence their decisions.

While most of the debate so far has focused on the wisdom of expansion and whether three or five new members was most appropriate, some experts say the question for many Americans is likely to be more basic.

"I don't think anyone in the administration has recognised this yet but the fact is that the debate about expansion is really going to call into question the need for the alliance after the Cold War," said Charles King, an assistant professor at Georgetown Universaity's School of Foreign Service.

A State Department official who was interviewed by an American radio station Wednesday was asked to explain to listeners in 38 Midwestern states the most basic elements of NATO -- what it is and what it does.
Under Article 5 of the NATO charter, an attack on one alliance members is considered an attack on all members. Member states are bound to defend their allies in such cases.

That means the United States is committed to send troops, if necessary, to fight for Luxembourg, Greece and Turkey, as well as France and Britain and nine other states. Expansion pushes that commitment to the borders of Ukraine and Belarus.

But the need for NATO, established as a military alliance after the Second World War to ensure security in Europe against the Soviet Union, is not always apparent now that the Soviet Union has disintegrated and communism is no more.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, along with other officials, has acknowledged that NATO "does not regard any state as its adversary" and would remain open in the future to membership by all European states, including Russia.
So where is the threat? Why retain NATO at all?
As a broader U.S. debate heats up, even advocates of expansion are raising tough questions.

One of these, North Carolina Sen. Jesse Helms, Republican chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Comittee, is concerned Clinton's expansion plan "may be evolving into a dangerous and ill-considered plan for NATO transformation ... into a new diluted NATO, converted from a well-defined military alliance into a nebulous collective security arrangement."

He and 19 other senators wrote Clinton a letter in which they pose questions they say he must answer before the Senate can vote on enlargement. Two-thirds of the 100-seat Senate -- or 67 votes -- are needed to approve the agreement.

Among them is what military threat NATO expansion is designed to counter, how expansion increases U.S. and European security and whether border disputes involving one or several of the new alliance members would be so vital a security threat that "we are willing to risk American lives."
With the United States the lead nation in NATO, Washington has a vested interest in retaining the alliance, its essential link to Europe, administration officials say.
Also, proponents feel strongly that NATO was so successful at keeping peace for over 40 years, it must be kept in place as an insurance against an unexpected new enemy.

Further, officials argue the alliance creates a stability that helps foster democracy and free market economies, as well as provides a vehicle for combating unconventional threats, like instability in Bosnia, terrorism and drug traffickers.
Ultimately, the betting is Clinton will win the two-thirds Senate vote allowing NATO to expand for the first time since communism collapsed.
